1.text: Categories such as synthesis, decomposition, and double displacement are used to describe reactions.

a.text: Precipitation reactions are common examples of double displacement reactions.

b.text: Removal of waters of hydration of ionic solids is a category of reactions that finds common use in introductory chemistry laboratory classes.

2.text: Oxidation–reduction reactions are important and include combustion.

a.text: Oxidation–reduction reactions are important to chemistry and are sometimes referred to as “redox” reactions.

b.text: Being able to identify an oxidation–reduction reaction often involves assigning oxidation numbers.

c.text: The use of oxidation–reduction reactions as a category includes the concepts of oxidizing and reducing agents.

d.text: Completion and balancing of oxidation–reduction reactions requires both mass and charge balance and is often facilitated by the concept of a half-reaction.

e.text: The oxidation–reduction of metals (with each other or with acids) yields a measure of the activities of metals.

f.text: Materials that are combustible are undergoing oxidation –reduction reactions, often with oxygen in air.

3.text: Acid–base neutralization is an important category of reaction s that includes several definitions.

a.text: Categorizing reactions in terms of acid–base chemistry, particularly in water, is important.

b.text: Categorizing acid–base reactions can be facilitated by a basic understanding of acid–base strength.

c.text: The definition of an acid as a proton donor and a base as a proton acceptor is a key concept of acid–base chemistry.

d.text: The definition of an acid as an electron-pair acceptor (Lewis acid) and a base as an electron-pair donor (Lewis base) is a key concept of acid– base chemistry.

organic.text: Addition, elimination, rearrangement, substitution, and redox reactions represent broad categories that are helpful in understanding organic reactions.
Key categories of organic reactions that students should be able to recognize include: SN1, SN2, E1, E2, and electrophilic and nucleophilic aromatic substitution.

Nucleophilic substitution occurs when a nucleophile displaces a leaving group. Bimolecular substitution (SN2) occurs via a concerted mechanism in which the nucleophile directly displaces the leaving group. Unimolecular substitution (SN1) occurs when the leaving group first leaves in a rate-determining step, followed by nucleophilic attack at the resultant carbocation intermediate.

Bimolecular (SN2) and unimolecular (SN1) nucleophilic substitution reactions compete with elimination reactions (E2 and E1, respectively). Preference for substitution or elimination is governed by steric hindrance and basicity of the reagent.

Elimination reactions (E2 and E1) occur via beta deprotonation to the site of the leaving group displacement. The resultant electron pair after deprotonation forms a π-bond with the carbon at the site of leaving group displacement. Elimination reactions occur in the presence of a strong base nucleophile.
SN1 reactions result in racemization (or near racemization) at the site of displacement due to the attack of the planar carbocation from above or below.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution is a reaction between an electrophile and an aromatic compound (electron-rich component). The electrophile replaces hydrogen on the aromatic species. Electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions include bromination, nitration, sulfonation, Friedel–Crafts alkylation, and acylation.
Nucleophilic substitution occurs via an addition–elimination or elimination–addition mechanism. Electrophilic substitution occurs exclusively via an addition-elimination mechanism.
Radical reactions, which show single electron movement, represent another broad category.

Radical reactions are regioselective, dependent on the stability of all possible reactive intermediates. More than one product is possible for a radical reaction; products (two or more) are labeled major or minor corresponding to predicted or observed relative yields.
Radical reactions follow a sequence of initiation, propagation, and termination steps.
It is important to recognize reaction conditions in an environmentally responsible (green) manner whenever possible.

inorganic.text: Many constructs involving atom and electron exchange have been developed to aid in our understanding of acid-base reactions.

In certain classification schemes, acids and bases are viewed as electron transfer between reactants. In the Lewis concept, the base donates an electron pair to the acid resulting in the formation of a coordinate covalent bond. The Usanovich concept involves electrons being transferred from the base to the acid in a reaction that forms a salt. Hard-soft acid base theory includes the effect of polarizability on the equilibrium position of Lewis acid-base reactions.

Acid base reactions can also be viewed as a transfer of an ionic species between the reactants. Examples include the Bronsted-Lowry definitions based on proton transfer and the Lux-Flood system based on oxide transfer reactions.

Autoionization reactions occur within many solvents to produce ionic products, and within solvent system classification schemes, acids and bases are defined as species that increase the concentrations of the cationic or anionic autoionization products, respectively, upon dissolution. The Arrhenius description is an example of a solvent system classification applied to aqueous solutions.
Oxidation-reduction reactions involve electron transfer between reactants to form products.
Reduction and oxidation processes result in a decrease and increase, respectively, of the oxidation states of the atoms involved.
An activity series can be used to predict whether a oxidation-reduction reaction will occur between two compounds.
Changes in oxidation states can be used to identify the reactants acting as oxidizing and reducing agents within oxidation/reduction reactions.

Many elements have a variety of accessible oxidation states in their compounds, and graphic representations are often used to aid in the understanding of the relative stability of these oxidation states under different reaction conditions. Examples include Latimer, Pourbaix, Frost, and Ellingham diagrams.
The reduction potential for a half reaction is related to the relative stabilities of the oxidation states of the reactants and products.

Disproportionation reactions are redox reactions involving a reactant in an intermediate oxidation state forming products in higher and lower oxidation states. Comproportionation reactions involve two reactants in different oxidation states reacting to form a product in a more stable intermediate oxidation state.

The reactions of organometallic compounds can be classified based on the electron count and coordination geometries of the reactants and products. Catalytic cycles involving organometallic species can be described using the terminology associated with these basic reaction types.

Oxidative addition reactions involve the addition of a reagent that increases the coordination number and decreases the oxidation state of the metal center. The reverse reaction is called reductive elimination.
Ligand association and dissociation reactions respectively increase or decrease the coordination number of a metal center without a change in oxidation state.

A migratory insertion usually involves a neutral ligand with a pi-system reacting with an anionic ligand to produce a new anionic ligand that has a new sigma-bond between the two. The reverse reaction is called an elimination reaction.
According to the Chauvin mechanism, alkene metathesis reactions involving alkylidene complexes typically proceed through a metallocyclobutyl intermediate.
Several reactions can be described as an attack of an outer sphere nucleophile or electrophile on a coordinated ligand.
The type of reaction(s) possible for an organometallic complex depend on the relative coordinative saturation/desaturation and valence electron count of the metal center.
Catalytic cycles involving organometallic complexes typically involve multiple bond breaking and formation reactions.
Double displacement, or metathesis, reactions between compounds involve an exchange of counterions between the reactants to form products.
Precipitation reactions produce an insoluble solid in the net ionic reaction.
Arrhenius acid-base reactions produce water as a product in the net ionic reaction.
Heterogenous processes often involve interactions of molecules with the surfaces of solids.
Physical adsorption, or physisorption, involves molecules being attracted to surface by van der Waals forces.
Chemical adsorption, or chemisorption, involves a species forming a chemical bond with a surface atom.
Surface migration allows chemisorbed species to move around on the solid surface.

Condensation reactions involve a combination of two molecules to form a larger molecule and release a much smaller molecule, such as water. Hydrolysis reactions involve reaction of water with a larger molecule to decompose it into smaller fragments.

physical.text: Molecularity provides an important characterization in the study of reactions and their rates.
Regardless of stoichiometric ratios, most individual reactions are either unimolecular or bimolecular.

E.text: Many chemical properties of elements follow periodic trends that can be used to strategically design reactions to achieve desired outcomes.

1.text: With some exceptions, elements in a single group or row on the periodic table have reactivity trends that vary in predictable ways when reacting with water or air.

a.text: Reactivity trends vary in predictable ways as you move down and to the right on the periodic table, with a few exceptions.

organic.text: Organic chemistry can be understood by studying the structure and reactivity of different functional groups. Reactions can be understood in collections by functional groups, collections including reactions leading to formation of functional groups, and reactions using the given functional group to form other functional groups. While key reactions of functional groups can be listed, such lists are not intended to be exhaustive within this map.
Key reactions of alkanes include combustion and free radical halogenation.
Key reactions of alkyl halides include SN1 and SN2 substitution, E1 and E2 elimination, and the formation of organometallic reagents.
Key reactions that include alkenes are reduction to alkanes, Diels– Alder, formation of alkyl halides, electrophilic addition, free radical reactions, and oxidative cleavage reactions.
Alkynes undergo many of the same reactions as alkenes, and can also be selectively reduced to cis- or trans-alkenes.
Key reactions of alcohols include oxidation to aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids, conversion to a chloride using sulfonyl chloride, and dehydration to form alkenes.
Key reactions of ethers include their formation by the Williamson ether synthesis and their reduction to alkyl halides.

Epoxides are highly reactive heterocyclic compounds; their key reactions include their formation via peroxy acid conditions and stereoselective opening in the presence of a strong acid or nucleophile.

Aromatic systems display a fairly broad array of important reactions, including: electrophilic or nucleophilic substitution; the oxidation of benzyl hydrogens to ketones, aldehydes, and carboxylic acids; reduction of aromatic nitro groups; and reactions of atoms that are alpha to aromatic rings, such as oxidation.

Aldehydes and ketones undergo many of the same key reactions, including: conversion to acetals; reduction to a –CH2– group via imine intermediates; combination into alkenes using Wittig reagents; nucleophilic attack at the carbonyl carbon; aldol and Claisen (reactions that depend on the acidity of hydrogens on the carbon alpha to the carbonyl group); conversion to complex alcohols by nucleophilic attack of organomagnesium and organocuprates; reduction to alcohols by hydride donors or Grignard reagents; and alpha-substitutions via basic and acidic conditions.

Key reactions of carboxylic acids and their derivatives include: interconversion via an addition–elimination mechanism; conversion to ketones or aldehydes by nucleophilic attack by organomagnesium; organocuprates; decarboxylation at high temperatures when the carboxylic acid group is beta to carbonyl groups; and conversion to enols or enolates when beta-carbonyl groups are present.
Key reactions of amines include their formation via substitution chemistry and Hoffman elimination reactions.

Substituents on an aromatic ring either activate or deactivate the ring (i.e., increase or decrease the electron density and susceptibility to electrophilic attack). Also, substituents serve to direct the adding group to an ortho, para, or meta relationship to it via resonance (electronic effect) stabilization of mechanistic intermediates, or via inductive effects.
The control of a reaction is important and is affected by time, temperature, catalysts, and solvent, etc.

inorganic.text: The half reaction reduction potentials for the elements follow a periodic trend.
Metals on the left side of the periodic table are strong reducing agents and nonmetals on the right side of the periodic table are strong oxidizing agents.
The reducing/oxidizing properties of elements strongly influence their terrestrial occurrence and extraction.
The hydration enthalpies of transition metal ions show a systematic variation with the ligand field stabilization energy associated with the aqua complex of the ion.
Acid base properties for similar compounds show systematic variations that follow periodic trends.
The acidity of an oxoacid is dependent on the number of oxo groups and the electronegativity of the central atom. The equilibrium constants for oxoacids can be estimated using Pauling's rules.
The acidity of binary acids varies with the size and electronegativity of the non-hydrogen atom.

There is a periodic variation of the acid-base character displayed by elements in aqueous solutions in which the oxidation state of the central atom determines where it lies on an aqua- hydroxo-oxo continuum.

The main group oxides show a systematic variation in acid-base properties across the period. Metal oxides react with water to produce basic solutions and nonmetal oxides react with water to produce acidic solutions. Amphoteric properties are displayed by the oxides of the semi-metallic elements in a group.
Polyoxoanions are formed from condensation reactions involving early transition metal oxo and hydroxo compounds.
The reactivity of Lewis acids and bases is influenced by steric and electronic effects, specifically including electron-withdrawing and electron-donating groups.

F.text: Chemical change can be controlled by choices of reactants, reaction conditions, or use of catalysts.

1.text: Utilizing solubility and/or precipitation reactions allows for the qualitative analysis of ions present in a solution.

a.text: Predicting the reactivity of chemicals is a key skill that can involve knowledge of solubility rules.

2.text: Control of chemical reactions is often not fully accomplished, so details such as limiting reactants and percentage yields are important in characterizing what occurs.

a.text: Stoichiometric calculations must determine the limiting reactant when it is not clear that some reactant(s) are present in excess.

b.text: Stoichiometric calculations provide the theoretical yield, which can be used to determine percentage yield.

organic.text: Different reagents or reaction conditions can control the regio- and stereochemistry of a reaction.
Different reagents or reaction conditions can control the regiochemistry of a reaction. 

inorganic.text: Examples of control include sterics, sol-gels, surface adsorption, particle size, size of ligands, pH, solvent effects
The Nernst equation can be used to determine the effect of nonstandard conditions (including pH) on an electrochemical cell potential.

Solvents play an important role in the observed kinetic behavior of reactions. For example, solutions containing solvated electrons can be prepared by dissolving alkali and alkaline earth metals in ammonia.
Phase diagrams can be used to predict the products of reactions under different conditions.
The reactivity of acids and bases is affected by the presence of sterically encumbered functional groups.
Latimer, Frost, and Pourbaix diagrams can be used in the selection of appropriate reagents for reduction-oxidation reactions.
Coordinative saturation plays an important role in the reactivity of many chemical compounds.
Organometallic compounds are synthesized by reaction of appropriate metal and ligand containing compounds.
Templating reactions involve combination of ligands within the inner sphere of a coordination complex. This type of reaction can be used to make macrocyclic ligands.
Metal containing compounds are often used as homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts for chemical reactions.
Zeolites and other porous solids have high surface areas and can be used to introduce shape selectivity.
Many heterogenous reactions employ high temperature and pressure conditions due to the high activation energies involved.
Homogeneous catalysts have been developed for a many chemical reactions, including hydroformylation, carbonylation, hydrogenation, oxidation, and olefin metathesis.
Metals are important in many biochemical processes.
Metal atoms can play structural, catalytic, or redox roles in biological systems. Examples include chlorophyll, hemoglobin, cytochrome C, and zinc containing biomolecules.
Chiral catalysts can be used control the stereochemistry of products of chemical reactions.
The acid base properties of a compound can be altered in nonaqueous solvents.
The levelling effect determines whether an acid or base will behave as a strong or weak electrolyte.
Superacids are acids stronger than sulfuric acid which can be employed in reactions requiring protonation of hydrocarbons.
Interesting compounds of the elements can be synthesized using fluorine and similar strong oxidizing agents.
Compounds of the noble gases are prepared from reaction with fluorine at high pressure and temperature.
The trans effect and trans influence can be used strategically in the synthesis of coordination compounds.
The trans effect refers to the dependence of the site dependent rate of ligand substitution on the ligand positioned trans to the departing ligand.
The trans influence refers to the impact of a ligand on the strength of the bond located in the trans position.
While the trans effect is most often discussed in the context of square planar complexes, it also has an effect in the reactivity of octahedral and five-coordinate complexes.
The presence of chelating ligands within the coordination sphere may influence the geometry of the products formed.
Hard-soft acid-base theory can be used to control the products of chemical reactions.
"Hard" species are small, nonpolarizable, and ionic; "soft" species are large, polarizable, and covalent.
Hard/Hard and Soft/Soft interactions are more energetically favorable than Hard/Soft interactions.
Choice of appropriate Hard/Soft metal/ligand combinations can lead to the desired product.
Hard ions tend to be lithophiles while soft ions tend to be chalcophiles within the Goldschmidt classification.
Hard-soft principles govern the formation of complexes containing ambidentate ligands.
Photochemical reactions are initiated using electromagnetic radiation, most commonly in the ultraviolet or visible range.

physical.text: Changing reaction conditions affects the chemical potential which determines the equilibrium position.
Chemical potential reflects the important variables of the free energy and thus is sensitive to the reaction conditions.
Reactions from nanochemistry often have different behaviors than bulk quantity reactions of the same materials.
The size of nanoparticles that are synthesized often depends on the reaction conditions.
Some reactions can be influenced by changes in total pressure.
When there is a net production or consumption of gases in a reaction, total pressure will influence the equilibrium location.
The identity of reaction products cannot be changed by the addition of a catalyst.
The presence of a catalyst does not affect the products formed or the equilibrium constant, only the rate of the reaction.

1.text: Modern materials represent an important example of the synthesis of new materials.

a.text: Some solid-state modern materials, including those that compose applications such as LEDs, do not require whole-number stoichiometry.

inorganic.text: Properties of solid state materials are dependent upon reaction conditions.
Solid materials are typically prepared by direct combination, reaction in solution, or sol gel methods.
The degree of crystallinity of a solid or thin film can be controlled by employing different reaction conditions.
The shape of nanomaterials is highly influenced by the reaction conditions employed.
Metal oxides are used in the production of glasses to impart different properties to the final product.
Synthesis of inorganic compounds often employs air, water, and light sensitive techniques.
Schlenk and dry box techniques are often employed when working with air and moisture sensitive compounds.
The principles of coordination chemistry can be employed in the design and synthesis of self- assembled monolayers, metal organic frameworks, inorganic polymers, and other related compounds.
A self-assembled monolayer is an organized two-dimensional structure formed by interactions of long-chained molecules with a surface.
Coordination polymers are formed when metal ions react with polydentate ligands to form extended structures.
Metal-organic frameworks are ordered coordination polymers which often possess large pores within their structures.

physical.text: Catalysis affects only reactions under kinetic control, not thermodynamic control.
In some reactions, a less stable product may be formed, because the activation energy is lower on the pathway that leads to that product.

VI.title: Energy and Thermodynamics
VI.text: Energy and Thermodynamics: Energy is the key currency of chemical reactions in molecular-scale systems as well as macroscopic systems.

A.text: Most chemical changes are accompanied by a net change of energy of the system.

lens_texts.general: Most chemical changes are accompanied by a net change of energy of the system.
lens_texts.organic: Most chemical changes are accompanied by a net change of energy of the system.
lens_texts.inorganic: Most chemical changes are accompanied by a net change of energy of the system.
lens_texts.physical: Most chemical changes are accompanied by a net change of energy of the system.

1.text: The role of kinetic versus potential energy is a key aspect of understanding how energy plays a role in chemical reactions.

2.text: Energy changes can be considered in terms of heat and work.

a.text: Concepts related to energy in chemistry require careful definitions that are more precise than are used in everyday language.

b.text: In thermodynamic treatments of chemical systems, the definition of the system of interest versus the surroundings is important.

3.text: There are a wide variety of energy units, so care must be taken to use consistent units when considering energy changes quantitatively.

4.text: Within thermodynamics, it is important to distinguish between internal energy (the heat associated with a constant volume process) and enthalpy (the heat associated with a constant pressure process).

organic.text: Thermodynamics is important in explaining energy changes.
Energy diagrams provide an important tool for understanding and illustrating reaction energetics.
Energies for reactants, intermediates, and products can be combined to model energy diagrams for reaction mechanisms.

inorganic.text: A spontaneous process is indicated by a negative Gibb's free energy for that process.
The equilibrium established between two different states is a function of the Gibb's free energy difference between the states.
Hess's Law can be used to calculate the lattice energy or heat of formation of an ionic solid from a Born-Haber cycle.

physical.text: The careful study of energy implications for reactions requires the definition of the system and its surroundings and their ability to exchange energy.
The system is the part of the universe in which we are interested and the surroundings are everything else, but practically the region outside of the system where pertinent measurements can be made.
Systems may be open, closed or isolated depending on where matter or energy can be exchanged with the surroundings.
Boundaries that permit energy flow between the system and surroundings are called diathermic and those that do not are called adiabatic.
Conservation of energy requires that energy changes of a system are matched by those of the surroundings.
Because reactions will most often have reactants and products that differ in energy, they exchange that energy difference with the surroundings.
Energy itself is neither created nor destroyed, so the amount of energy lost (or gained) by the system is gained (or lost) by the surroundings.
Endothermic reactions absorb energy from and exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings
Measurements generally provide changes in energy rather than absolute energy, so sign conventions have been devised to distinguish energy release from energy absorption by the system.
Energy changes that occur during chemical changes can be measured (using calorimetry).
Under proper conditions, the energy change in the system can be determined by measuring a temperature change using a calorimeter, an apparatus that attempts to isolate the heat flow.

B.text: Many chemical reactions require an energy input to be initiated.

lens_texts.general: Many chemical reactions require an energy input to be initiated.
lens_texts.organic: Many chemical reactions require an energy input to be initiated.
lens_texts.inorganic: Many chemical reactions require an energy input to be initiated.
lens_texts.physical: Many chemical reactions require an energy input to be initiated.

1.text: Reactive chemicals may remain stable for long times because the reactions they undergo must be initiated by some form of energy input, such as a spark or flame.

organic.text: Reactions generally require an input of energy to overcome the energy of activation.

inorganic.text: Activation energy for a reaction determines the rate at which a reaction occurs at a given temperature.
A catalyst decreases the activation energy for a reaction by enabling a different mechanistic pathway.
An activated complex with higher energy than reactants or products is usually formed during the course of a reaction.
There are examples of reactions that do not require energy to initiate the process.

Many inorganic compounds are fluxional at room temperature because the activation energy associated with structural distortion is low. Dynamic NMR experiments are often employed to measure the activation energy for these processes.
Activation energies for substitution in transition metal coordination complexes can be influenced by the ligand field stabilization energy. (e.g. water exchange rates)

physical.text: Energy input may come from a variety of sources and is required to overcome the activation energy.
Activation energy may be supplied by any of several methods, such as flames, electrical discharge, light or molecular collisions.
Reactive chemicals may be in contact and not react, because initial energy input is required to start the reaction.
Hydrocarbon fuels can be stored in the presence of air and not react with the oxygen present until a spark or flame provides the initial energy.

C.text: The type of energy associated with chemical change may be heat, light, or electrical energy.

lens_texts.general: The type of energy associated with chemical change may be heat, light, or electrical energy.
lens_texts.organic: The type of energy associated with chemical change may be heat, light, or electrical energy.

1.text: Heat exchange is measured via temperature change.

a.text: Heat flow into the system is defined as endothermic; heat flow out of the system is defined as exothermic.

b.text: Heat flow is quantitatively obtained from T via molar heat capacity or specific heat and the mass of the substance involved.

c.text: By convention, numerical estimates of exothermic processes carry a negative sign, while endothermic processes carry a positive sign.

d.text: When observed in the laboratory, exothermic processes will show warming (heat evolved), while endothermic processes will show cooling (heat absorbed).

2.text: The enthalpy of reaction is a measure of heat exchange for reactions carried out at constant pressure.

a.text: Enthalpies of reaction, such as those incorporated in a thermochemical equation, can be used to calculate energy flow for a given amount of reactant or product.

3.text: Electrochemistry is predicated on oxidation–reduction reactions, and involves physically separating the electron production of oxidation from the electron consumption of reduction.

a.text: Oxidation–reduction reactions can be considered in two halves, and can be physically separated to form electrochemical systems.

b.text: Electrical energy can be obtained from electrochemical systems operating as galvanic cells.

organic.text: Heat and light are common types of energy associated with reactions.
The source of energy input can affect mechanisms and change the products of pericyclic reactions.

inorganic.text: Many chemical and biochemical processes interconvert chemical energy with other forms of energy.
Light energy can be used to photodissociate chemical bonds.
Bioluminescent and chemiluminescent processes produce light from chemical energy, while photosynthetic process use light to effect chemical change.
Methods exist to measure or estimate energy differences within a system or a portion of the system.

physical.text: Heat provides reaction energy by increasing the number of fast moving molecules and therefore high energy collisions.
Heat transfer into a reaction system increases the temperature and therefore increases the average speed of the molecules present.
Photochemical reactions use light energy to initiate a reaction.
In photochemical reactions, a reactant absorbs light which often creates a reactive species that then initiates further reactions.
Electrical energy may either initiate a reaction or be generated by a reaction.
When electrical energy is produced by a reaction it may be used to power a galvanic cell.
Electrolysis occurs when electrical energy is an input that causes a reaction.
The Gibbs energy represents the maximum electrical work obtainable from a chemical reaction.
Some reactions release light as a product.
Products in chemical may be created in an excited state that releases energy as light, causing luminescence.
Fluorescence occurs when the light released occurs on a relatively short time scale and arises from allowed electronic transitions.
Phosphorescence occurs when the light released occurs on a relatively long time scale and arises from non-allowed electronic transitions.

D.text: Breaking chemical bonds requires energy; formation of chemical bonds releases energy.

lens_texts.general: Breaking chemical bonds requires energy; formation of chemical bonds releases energy.
lens_texts.organic: Breaking chemical bonds requires energy, and formation of chemical bonds releases energy.
lens_texts.inorganic: Breaking chemical bonds requires energy and formation of chemical bonds releases energy
lens_texts.physical: Breaking chemical bonds requires energy and formation of chemical bonds releases energy.

1.text: While breaking a chemical bond is always endothermic, chemical energy can be released via reactions because bonds are both broken and formed in the course of the reaction.

a.text: The extent of energy release or absorption is dictated by the bonds broken in the reactants and the bonds formed in the products.

organic.text: In a reaction, often there is both bond breaking and bond formation, so the energy consequences depend on both.
The transition state of an SN2 reaction has concurrent bond making and bond breaking.

inorganic.text: Born-Haber cycles typically include the effect of bond dissociation enthalpy on the lattice energy of an ionic compound.
The activation energy for a reaction is often determined by bond dissociation energies.
Proton gain enthalpies are often used to measure and explain acid and base strength.
The identities of the metal and ligand are important to the energies observed in the reactions of coordination complexes.
Bond energies are often affected by ligand field stabilization energy in coordination complexes.
In dissociatively activated reactions, a linear free energy relationship typically exists between the log of the rate constant and the log of the equilibrium constant.

physical.text: Reactions are either exothermic or endothermic based on which bonds are broken and which bonds form.
Any chemical bond releases energy upon formation or absorbs energy when broken, but chemical reactions include both breaking and forming of bonds, so they may be either endothermic or exothermic.

E.text: The forces that are associated with energy change in chemical processes are electrostatic forces.

lens_texts.general: The forces that are associated with energy change in chemical processes are electrostatic forces.
lens_texts.organic: The forces that are associated with energy change in chemical processes are electrostatic forces.
lens_texts.inorganic: The forces that are associated with energy change in chemical processes are electrostatic forces.
lens_texts.physical: The forces that are associated with energy change in chemical processes are electrostatic forces.

1.text: Moving charge in an external circuit (electrochemistry) provides one lever by which this concept is measured.

a.text: When an electrochemical system is built, it is possible to determine the cell potential.

b.text: Trends related to cell potential are summarized via tables of standard reduction potentials.

c.text: Calculations using standard reduction potentials can determine cell potential and the spontaneous direction of an electrochemical reaction.

d.text: Nonstandard situations are addressed via the Nernst equation.

e.text: External electrical energy can be used to drive an electrochemical system in the nonspontaneous direction. Quantitative information about stoichiometry of these systems can be derived from variables related to electricity flow.

organic.text: Interactions with solvent can be described in terms of dipole–dipole or induced-dipole interactions.

inorganic.text: The potential of an electrochemical cell can be related to Gibb's free energy for the cell reaction.
Half reaction potentials are used to calculate the standard cell potential for a chemical reaction. The Nernst Equation can be used to calculate cell potentials for non-standard conditions.
Electrostatic forces play an important role in the formation of coordination complexes.

The Irving-Williams series determines the effect of metal ion on the formation constant for octahedral coordination complexes, and results from a combination of electrostatic attraction due to increasing effective nuclear charge and ligand field stabilization energy of the electron configuration associated with the metal ion.
The Drago-Wayland equation is used to estimate the enthalpy of a reaction based on electrostatic and covalent factors.

physical.text: The Coulomb forces present in molecules give rise to potential energy that can be divided into electronic, vibrational and rotational components.
The electronic potential energy arises from all pairwise Coulomb forces between electrons and protons.
Within the Born-Oppenheimer approximation, the nuclear motions associated with vibrations arise from the potential energy established by the electron distributions around the nuclei.
In addition to internal motions of electrons, and of vibration, the whole molecule may rotate or translate in space.
Electrochemical reactions directly tap the electrostatic nature of forces to do electrical work.
Oxidation reduction reactions have a net movement of electrons, and when carried out with some form of separation, the electron flow can be harnessed to do electrical work.

F.text: In accord with thermodynamics, energy is conserved in chemical changes, but the change of form in which the energy is present may be harnessed via natural or human-made devices.

lens_texts.general: In accord with thermodynamics, energy is conserved in chemical changes, but the change of form in which the energy is present may be harnessed via natural or human-made devices.
lens_texts.organic: In accord with thermodynamics, energy is conserved in chemical changes, but the change of form in which the energy is present may be harnessed via natural or human-made devices.
lens_texts.inorganic: In accord with thermodynamics, energy is conserved in chemical changes, but the change of form in which the energy is present may be harnessed via natural or man-made devices.
lens_texts.physical: In accord with thermodynamics, energy is conserved in chemical changes, but the change of form in which the energy is present may be harnessed via natural or man-made devices.

1.text: Pressure–volume (PV) work is a common means by which chemical changes, particularly combustion, are harnessed in human -made devices.

2.text: Electrochemical cells provide one way that chemical change is harnessed in human-made devices (batteries).

a.text: Batteries and fuels cells are important applications of electrochemical systems.

organic.text: Hydrocarbon compounds are commonly combusted for energy.

inorganic.text: Galvanic cells, such as batteries or fuel cells, can be used to produce electrical energy from chemical energy, while electrolytic cells are use electrical energy to effect chemical change.
Diagrams representing electrochemical cells show the chemical identity of the anode and cathode, solution contents, and the direction of electron flow.
Line notation can also be used to represent the contents of an electrochemical cell.
Several devices exist for the conversion of electrical energy to other forms of energy.
Thermoelectric materials are used to interconvert heat and electrical energy.
Photoelectric and electro-optic materials are capable of interconverting light and electrochemical energy. Common examples include solar cells and light emitting diodes.
Piezoelectric materials are used to interconvert electrical and mechanical energy.

physical.text: The efficiency of engines is fundamentally limited as dictated by the 2nd Law of Thermodynamics.
One key statement of the second law of thermodynamics is that no process can occur where the only result is the complete conversion of heat energy into work.
Efficiency of a heat engine, defined as the ratio of work performed to heat absorbed, is maximized for a reversible engine.
Refrigeration does work to transfer heat, and the efficiency is captured by the coefficient of performance which is the inverse of the efficiency of a heat engine.
Efficiency may be improved by increasing the temperature of the hot reservoir or decreasing the temperature of the cold reservoir or both.
Converting heat into work in a system requires the production of waste heat into the surroundings.
Work is path dependent because of the production of waste heat.

G.text: Thermodynamics provides a detailed capacity to understand energy change at the macroscopic level.

lens_texts.general: Thermodynamics provides a detailed capacity to understand energy change at the macroscopic level.
lens_texts.organic: Thermodynamics provides a detailed capacity to understand energy change at the macroscopic level.
lens_texts.inorganic: Thermodynamics provides a detailed capacity to understand energy change at the macroscopic level.

1.text: A key concept within thermodynamics is the state function, which can be defined as a quantity whose value is independent of its history.

a.text: Standard states of substances play a key role in thermodynamic calculations.

2.text: Hess’s law takes advantage of enthalpy being a state function to allow the determination of enthalpy change for a reaction based on combinations of more readily measured, or tabulated, reaction enthalpies.

a.text: Enthalpy is a key thermodynamic state function for calculation of heat exchange for many processes; these calculations include Hess’s law.

b.text: Tabulated values for the calculation of thermodynamic variables often take advantage of the concept of the formation reaction.

c.text: The concept of Hess’s law is useful in calculating thermodynamic properties from both reactions and tabulated values.

organic.text: Bond energies of reactants and products can be used to estimate macroscopic enthalpy changes for reactions.

inorganic.text: Bond dissociation energies can be used to calculate the enthalpy change of a reaction.

physical.text: Heat flows from a warmer body to a cooler body until thermal equilibrium is established.

The zeroth law of thermodynamics indicates that if system A is in thermal equilibrium with system B and B is in thermal equilibrium with system C, then system A is in thermal equilibrium with C as well.
The zeroth law provides the basis of using a thermometer to measure temperature.
0 K is defined as the temperature at which the molar volume of an ideal gas goes to zero.
The idea that the total energy of isolated systems is conserved, allows for mathematical expressions for the transformation of energy from one form to another.
The first law of thermodynamics states that the internal energy of an isolated system is constant, and because the universe is an isolated system, its energy must be constant.
Thermodynamic systems may be described as isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric or isochoric.
Systems that are not isolated will exchange energy with their surroundings, unless the boundary does not allow energy transfer, or the surroundings maintain thermal equilibrium with the system.
When a thermodynamic system is held at constant pressure it is said to be isobaric, and these conditions favor the use of specific state functions such as enthalpy or Gibbs Free Energy
When a thermodynamic system is held at constant volume it is said to be isochoric, and these conditions favor the use of specific state functions such as internal energy or Helmholtz Free Energy
A boundary that does not allow energy exchange as heat leads to an adiabatic system.
Systems that are maintained at constant temperature are called isothermal systems.

Expansion or compression of gases may be carried out under different conditions, such as free expansion, expansion or compression against a constant pressure or reversible expansion or compression and these conditions influence the calculation of work and heat.
Compression or expansion of a gas may be carried out under adiabatic or isothermal conditions, and these conditions influence the calculation of work and heat for the process.
Measurable primary thermodynamic functions are T, P, V and composition.
P, V, T, and n may, in principle, vary so must be measured or held constant in thermodynamic experiments and mathematical manipulations.
Measurable primary thermodynamic functions are related to other thermodynamic properties via partial derivative relationships.
Heat capacity, Cp, Cv are defined as derivatives of enthalpy and internal energy with respect to temperature and they provide a proportionality constant between heat and temperature change.
Isothermal compressibility is defined as the partial derivative of volume with respect to pressure (at constant temperature) multiplied by (-1/V).
The expansion coefficient is defined as the partial derivative of volume with respect to temperature (at constant pressure) multiplied by (1/V)
The Joule-Thomson coefficient is defined as the partial derivative of temperature with respect to pressure at constant enthalpy.
The isothermal Joule-Thomson coefficient is defined as the partial derivative of enthalpy with respect to pressure at constant temperature.
Work and heat are the main forms of energy exchange, and their sum is the internal energy.
Energy is defined as the capacity to do work.
Energy that exchanges because the system is in thermal contact with surroundings at a different temperature is called heat.
Work is defined by moving an object against an opposing force.
Work is associated with organized particle motion while heat is associated with random particle motion.
According to the first law of thermodynamics, the sum of heat and work equals the change of internal energy of the system.
The change in internal energy, ΔU, is measurable under constant volume conditions.
Internal energy is a state function and the change in internal energy equals the heat under constant volume conditions.
Bomb calorimetry maintains constant volume conditions, and therefore represents a method to measure the change in internal energy.
A perfect gas is identified by the fact that the partial derivative of its internal energy with respect to volume at constant temperature is zero.
Enthalpy is defined as U+PV and describes the heat flow under constant pressure conditions.
Enthalpy is a state function.
The change in enthalpy equals the heat under constant pressure conditions, and because these conditions are more common in the laboratory it is often the thermodynamic function used for heat.
Because enthalpy is a state function, Hess's Law states that reactions can be summed and/or tabulated values of the enthalpies of formation can be used to calculate ΔH .

So long as the temperature difference is not too large, the enthalpy change of a reaction at a temperature T1 may be estimated from the enthalpy change at T2, by adding the integral over T1 to T2 of the difference in molar heat capacities times dT.
State functions in thermodynamics are path independent, and many mathematical relationships are built upon this property.
The value of a state function depends only on its state, not the path by which that state was reached.
Mathematically, state functions have exact differentials.
Key examples of state functions include: S, T, P, H, V, n, G, A, while heat and work are important variables that are not state functions.
Thermodynamic cycles can be used to determine changes in values of state functions.
Thermodynamic calculations do not provide information about the rates of reactions.
Knowing that a particular system is more thermodynamically stable in one state than another provides no evidence as to the rate at which a change could occur.

H.text: The tendency of nature to disperse, particularly in terms of energy distribution, is embodied in the state function called entropy.

lens_texts.general: The tendency of nature to disperse, particularly in terms of energy distribution, is embodied in the state function called entropy.
lens_texts.organic: The tendency of nature to disperse, particularly in terms of energy distribution, is embodied in the state function called entropy.
lens_texts.inorganic: The tendency of nature to disperse, particularly in terms of energy distribution, is embodied in the state function called entropy.
lens_texts.physical: The tendency of nature to disperse, particularly in terms of energy distribution, is embodied in the state function called entropy.

1.text: Spontaneous changes will always increase the entropy of the universe (practically speaking—the entropy of the system and surroundings).

a.text: The definition of entropy and the ability to calculate change in entropy for a reaction are important.

b.text: A qualitative, conceptual understanding of processes that lead to more random physical distributions of particles with an increase in entropy is valuable.

c.text: An individual, nonspontaneous process can occur when linked to another process such that the combined events increase the entropy of the universe.

2.text: Gibb’s free energy is a state function that simultaneously calculates entropy for the system and surroundings, and is useful for determining whether or not a process occurs spontaneously.

a.text: Gibbs free energy is defined in such a way that the calculation of it provides insight into whether a process is spontaneous with a single calculation.

b.text: The Gibb’s free energy is defined in terms of enthalpy and entropy changes; students should be able to consider these components both quantitatively and qualitatively.

c.text: Calculations of Gibb’s free energy from tabulated values are important not only to obtain ΔG, but often to estimate equilibrium constants or cell potentials as well.

3.text: The entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K is 0.

a.text: Because the entropy has a specific value at 0 K, tabulated values for entropy need not be enumerated as changes relative to a standard reference state.

4.text: Thermodynamic spontaneity alone cannot predict whether a process will occur. Some spontaneous processes occur too slowly to be readily observed.

a.text: Even spontaneous processes may not be observed if there is a large activation energy for the process to begin.

inorganic.text: In chemical reactions where the changes in enthalpy are small, entropy can play a major role in predicting the direction of chemical reactions.

In the thermodynamic chelate effect, complexes containing polydentate ligands are favored in an equilibrium over complexes containing analogous monodentate ligands because formation of the chelated complexes results in an increase in entropy. An additional enthalpic term resulting from ligand pre-organization causes the macrocycle effect.
The Gibb's equation describes the change in free energy for a system with respect to the change in enthalpy plus the change in entropy times the temperature.
The temperature dependence of electrochemical cell potential can be used to calculate entropy of reaction.

physical.text: The direction of spontaneous change is towards the dispersal of energy into more disordered forms.
An increase in heat of a system is accompanied by a more disordered dispersal of the energy.
While more ordered systems can be created, the work required to do so is accompanied by an even greater amount of heat dispersal, so the overall change is towards more disordered forms of energy.
Entropy is a state function that reflects the dispersal of energy into disordered forms and can be defined in terms of either macroscopic variables (heat and temperature) or microstates.
Entropy change can be defined in terms of qrev/T.
Entropy can be defined in terms of microstates using the Boltzmann definition: S = k ln(W).
The entropy of any isolated system increases in a spontaneous change.
Because the universe is an isolated system, Δ Suniv increases for any spontaneous process.
For a system that is not isolated, the entropy change of the system and the surroundings must both be considered to determine the spontaneous direction of change.

Processes that do work are generally more ordered (at the particulate level) than heat flow processes, so creating work from heat sources is in the opposite direction as dictated by entropy of the system.
The relatively ordered nature of work when compared to heat justifies the macroscopic statement of the second law of thermodynamics that heat cannot be converted completely into work.
Perfect gases have no enthalpy change upon mixing, so the entire driving force for the spontaneous mixing of gases is due to the increase in entropy, i.e. a less ordered state.
The change in the Helmholtz Free Energy indicates if a process occurring at constant temperature and volume is spontaneous or not.
The Helmholtz Free Energy, A, is defined as A=U-TS
A process at constant volume and temperature will be spontaneous if the change in the Helmholtz free energy is negative or zero.
The change in the Gibbs Free Energy indicates if a process occurring at constant temperature and pressure is spontaneous or not.
The Gibbs Free Energy, G, is defined as G=H-TS
A process at constant pressure and temperature will be spontaneous if the change in the Gibbs free energy is negative or zero.

The definition of the Gibbs free energy essentially takes into account the entropy change of both the system and surroundings and allows the determination of the spontaneous direction of change via a single variable.
ΔG is the maximum amount of non-PV work.
Because the Gibbs Free Energy is a state function, summed reactions and/or tabulated values of the free energy of formation can be used to calculate ΔG.
The spontaneous direction of phase changes can be related to Gibbs energy and signs and relative sizes of ΔH and ΔS
The Third Law of Thermodynamics defines the absolute entropy scale.
Absolute entropies at a given T° can be calculated using the Third Law of Thermodynamics
Entropy can be calculated from the temperature dependence of the heat capacity.

I.text: Energy changes associated with nuclear chemistry are many orders of magnitude larger than those of classical chemical changes.

lens_texts.general: Energy changes associated with nuclear chemistry are many orders of magnitude larger than those of classical chemical changes.
lens_texts.organic: Energy changes associated with nuclear chemistry are many orders of magnitude larger than those of classical chemical change.
lens_texts.inorganic: Energy changes associated with nuclear chemistry are many orders of magnitude larger than those of classical chemical change.
lens_texts.physical: Energy changes associated with nuclear chemistry are many orders of magnitude larger than those of classical chemical change.

1.text: Basic concepts related to energy in nuclear reactions derive from the conversion of mass to energy.

a.text: Nuclear chemistry arises when there are changes in the nuclei of atoms.

b.text: Mass deficits in nuclear reactions arise from the conversion of mass to energy and are calculated via the equation: E = mc 2 .

c.text: Nuclear reactions give off radiation that may have biological effects.

inorganic.text: Nuclear energy levels are quantized, and transitions can occur between nuclear states to release energy. Nuclear fission and fusion reactions can be used to harness energy from these transitions.
The binding energy is a measure of the stability of a nuclear state with respect to free nucleons.
Concepts such as magic numbers, the even-odd rule, and the Island of Stability are used to rationalize the stability of certain isotopes in comparison with others.

physical.text: Energy of nuclear processes arises from mass changes and are calculated via E=mc2.
The mass deficit that arises in nuclear reactions leads to large energy changes via Einstein's equation.
Nuclear energy changes are much greater than energy changes associated with chemical changes.
