VII.title: Kinetics
VII.text: Kinetics: Chemical changes have a time scale over which they occur.

A.text: Chemical change can be measured as a function of time and occurs over a wide range of time scales.

lens_texts.general: Chemical change can be measured as a function of time and occurs over a wide range of time scales.
lens_texts.organic: Chemical change can be measured as a function of time and occurs over a wide range of time scales.
lens_texts.inorganic: Chemical change can be measured as a function of time and occurs over a wide range of time scales.
lens_texts.physical: Chemical change occurs over a wide range of time scales.

1.text: The rate of the reaction must be defined in a manner that is not dependent on which reactant or product is used to measure it.

a.text: The reaction rate should incorporate reaction stoichiometry when it is defined.

2.text: Rate is generally defined as the change in concentration of a reactant or product as a function of time.

a.text: Chemical reactions may occur at a wide range of rates, and a key aspect of rate is related to the concentration of species involved in the reaction.

3.text: When solids are included in reactions, surface area is an important factor in the rate of reaction.

a.text: A reactive solid with a large surface area will react more rapidly than the same solid with a smaller surface area.

organic.text: Differences between fast and slow reactions can play a vital role in determining what product forms in a reaction.

inorganic.text: Complexes are classified as inert or labile relative to the timescale that substitution reactions occur.
The relative rates of solvation for metal ions vary with the charge, size, and ligand field stabilization energy of the ion.
Fluxionality of complexes can occur and be observed at different timescales.

physical.text: Time scale for measuring or monitoring reaction rates must match the time scale on which a reaction occurs.
Some experiments may be studied using real-time analysis of the system composition while other reactions are studied using quenching methods.
Flow methods and stopped-flow methods provide access to different time ranges for reactions, with stopped-flow methods being used for faster reactions.
Relaxation methods can be used to study kinetics at the millisecond time scale.
Relaxation methods study the return of a system to an equilibrium state after a sudden change in conditions has perturbed that equilibrium system.
Temperature jump methods perturb the equilibrium with a change in temperature and pressure jump methods can be used with systems where equilibrium is sensitive to the total pressure.
Spectroscopic probes are often used to monitor concentration as a function of time.
Spectroscopic probes of reaction kinetics are particularly useful when one reactant or product has strong absorption properties in a particular spectral region.
Laser induced fluorescence is capable of providing state-specific monitoring of product molecules.
Multiphoton ionization techniques, often paired with mass spectrometric detection, can be used to monitor reaction dynamics.
Rates of reaction can vary depending on specific isotopes present.
The kinetic isotope effect refers to the decrease in reaction rate when a heavier isotope of an atom is present in a reactant.

The magnitude of the kinetic isotope effect is dependent on the ratio of the reduced masses between the heavier and lighter isotopes, thus the largest effect arises from replacing hydrogen with deuterium.

The primary kinetic isotope effect occurs when the rate determining step involves breaking a bond that includes the replaced isotope, while in the secondary kinetic isotope effect some other bond is broken in the rate determining step.
Rates of chemical reactions change over time.
Reaction rates can be determined as instantaneous or average rates.
The initial rate, an instantaneous rate measured at the start of a kinetics experiment, is often used to compare rates of different reactions.

B.text: Empirically derived rate laws summarize the dependence of reaction rates on concentrations of reactants and temperature.

lens_texts.general: Empirically derived rate laws summarize the dependence of reaction rates on concentrations of reactants and temperature.
lens_texts.organic: Empirically derived rate laws summarize the dependence of reaction rates on concentrations of reactants and temperature.
lens_texts.inorganic: Empirically derived rate laws summarize the dependence of reaction rates on concentrations of reactants and temperature.
lens_texts.physical: Empirically derived rate laws summarize the dependence of reaction rates on concentrations of reactants and temperature.

1.text: The “order” of a reaction is derived from the exponent on the concentration term of a given reactant in the rate law.

a.text: Rate laws are always determined experimentally, and the methods of initial rates or graphical depiction of rates provide the key method for determining rate laws.

b.text: Once known, a rate law can be used to quantitatively predict concentrations of species involved in a reaction as a function of time.

c.text: The kinetics of nuclear processes is first order and can be quantitatively treated, often by indicating the half-life of a nuclear reaction.

2.text: The temperature dependence of the reaction rate is contained in the rate constant. This temperature dependence is often well modeled by the Arrhenius model.

a.text: Under most circumstances, an increase in temperature leads to an increase in reaction rate.

b.text: Empirical fits of temperature data in kinetics can be used to estimate the activation energy.

organic.text: Rate laws can provide clues to reaction mechanisms, particularly substitution and elimination reactions.
Rate laws can be developed from reaction equations or reaction mechanisms.

inorganic.text: Kinetic information is obtained experimentally by measurement of reaction rate under a variety of conditions.
Concentration dependence is used to determine order and rate constant of a reaction at a particular temperature and pressure.
The Eyring equation is used to determine the enthalpy and entropy of activation from temperature dependent measurements of the rate constant.
The volume of activation is determined from pressure-dependent measurements of the rate constant.

physical.text: Many reactions have integer exponents for concentrations that are in the rate law leading to 1st order, 2nd order and 3rd order rate laws as commonly (but not exclusively) seen expressions.
The fundamental goal of the rate law is to summarize the effect of changes in concentration on the rate of a reaction.
The rate law expression can be integrated to derive an expression of concentration vs. time.
Complex rate laws may not have an integer order but can be experimentally forced into an order such as a pseudo 1st order or 2nd order reaction.
The units on the rate constant, k, reflect the order of the reaction.
In many cases, integrated rate laws can be determined by monitoring either reactant disappearance or product formation.
The isolation method uses large excess of all but one reactant to determine the pseudo-rate order of the reaction for that one (not excess) reactant.
Experimental data can provide either absolute or relative reaction rates.
Absolute reaction rates are best measured in systems where the reaction of interest is the only reaction taking place.
Reactive species, like radicals, often participate in more than one reaction, and the study of such systems may rely on measuring relative reaction rates for the various reactions.
One way to characterize the rate of a reaction is to define the half-life which is particularly useful in 1st order kinetics.
The half-life is defined as the time it takes for the concentration of a reactant to reach half its initial value.
The half-life in a first-order reaction does not depend on the concentration of the observed species and thus provides a convenient way to rank the rates of such reactions.
Reaction rates depend on temperature and this dependence can often be captured by using the Arrhenius equation for the rate constant.
For many reactions, a plot of the natural log of the rate constant versus inverse temperature provides a straight line and the reaction is said to display Arrhenius behavior.
The Arrhenius equation has two parameters, the pre-exponential or frequency factor and the activation energy, which can be obtained from fits to experimental data.

C.text: Most chemical reactions take place by a series of more elementary reactions, called the reaction mechanism.

lens_texts.general: Most chemical reactions take place by a series of more elementary reactions, called the reaction mechanism.
lens_texts.organic: Most chemical reactions take place by a series of more elementary reactions, called the reaction mechanism.
lens_texts.inorganic: Most chemical reactions take place by a series of more elementary reactions, called the reaction mechanism
lens_texts.physical: Most chemical reactions take place by a series of more elementary reactions, called the reaction mechanism.

1.text: The reaction stoichiometry does not imply the species actually involved in a reaction.

2.text: It is possible to devise a series of reactions that, when summed, yield the overall reaction and provide a mechanism for how the reaction occurs.

a.text: Chemical reactions often occur via multiple steps, called the reaction mechanism.

b.text: One step in a mechanism, the rate determining step, is often much slower than others and this slow step tends to determine the overall reaction rate.

c.text: Given a reaction mechanism and knowing the rate determining step allows the rate law to be inferred. This rate law must match the observed empirical rate law for a mechanism to be valid.

d.text: A compatible rate law does not “prove” the correctness of a mechanism.

e.text: Species that appear in a reaction mechanism but not in the overall reactions are called intermediates and their identification can provide important evidence about how well the mechanism describes the reaction.

organic.text: Reaction steps are fundamental to understanding each functional group’s reactivity in organic chemistry.
The slowest step is the rate-determining step.
Functional groups consist of polar or polarizable bonds that dictate reactivity.
Curved arrow mechanisms show electron movement from nucleophiles to electrophiles in elementary reactions.
Reaction mechanisms can de depicted illustrating the movement of electrons for every bond broken or formed.

inorganic.text: Most reaction mechanisms involve the reactants colliding to form an activated complex, or transition state, that proceeds to form the products of the reaction.
The properties of the solvent often influence the stability of the transition state.
Steady-state approximations are often used to understand the relationship of a multistep mechanism and the observed rate law.

Redox processes are classified as inner-sphere or outer-sphere based on the mechanism of electron transfer. Inner-sphere electron transfer takes place through chemical bonds while outer sphere reactions involve through space interactions.
Outer-sphere electron transfer displays kinetic behavior that can be interpreted using Marcus theory.

Substitution reactions of coordination complexes can be explained by associative (A), dissociative (D), and interchange (Ia, Id) mechanisms. Mechanisms are classified as associative or dissociative if an intermediate can be observed by experiment, while interchange reactions proceed through an unobservable transition state.
The role of the incoming, outgoing, and spectator ligands in determining reaction outcome and stereochemistry is used in classification of a mechanism as dissociative or associative.

The coordination environment of a metal influences the mechanism of ligand substitution observed. Substitution in octahedral complexes is typically dissociative, while substitution in square planar complexes is typically associative at high ligand concentrations and dissociative at low ligand concentrations.
The relative coordinative saturation of a metal center will affect the mechanism observed. Dissociative mechanisms are often observed in complexes containing sterically bulky ligands.
Activation volumes can be used as further evidence in the classification of a reaction mechanism as associative (ΔV > 0) or dissociative (ΔV < 0).
pH dependence of a reaction rate is used as evidence to support mechanisms involving protonation or deprotonation of ligands.
The Fuoss-Eigen equation allows for the estimation of an equilibrium constant for formation of an encounter complex in dissociative reactions.
Rates of dissociative substitution reactions often have rate dependent on the ligand field stabilization energy of the reactants.
Dissociative substitution reactions typically exhibit a linear free energy relationship between the log of the rate constant and the log of the equilibrium constant for bond dissociation.
Mechanisms for reorganization in fluxional complexes involve distortion of the bond angles within the complexes.
Fluxionality in trigonal pyramidal complexes is explained using the Berry pseudorotation mechanism.
Fluxionality in octahedral complexes is often explained using the Bailar or Ray-Dutt twist mechanisms.
The kinetic chelate effect is used to explain the stability of complexes with polydentate ligands.
Binding of the donor atoms of chelate complexes occurs at the same rate as monodentate ligand complexes.
Fast rebinding of the first dissociated donor atom of a chelate due to that atom's huge "effective concentration" is the source of the chelate effect.

The macrocycle effect is a greater stability of macrocyclic complexes than can be explained by the chelate effect. The cause is the slow dissociation of the first donor atom due to the additional rigidity of the macrocyclic ring.
The cryptate effect is a further enhancement of complex stability when two macrocyclic rings are fused, which further increases rigidity.

physical.text: Kinetics mechanisms sum the elementary reactions to achieve the overall reaction.
There may be numerous ways to envision elementary steps for a kinetic mechanism, but any possible mechanism must ultimately be summed to provide the overall reaction.
Reaction intermediates can be built up if the elementary step producing them is faster than those that are consuming them.
The molecularity of elementary steps defines how many particles collide in the reaction.
Three body collisions are not likely to occur, so virtually all elementary steps are either unimolecular or bimolecular.
For elementary reactions only, the rate law can be obtained directly from the stoichiometry to the reactant particles.
The Lindemann-Hinshelwood mechanism provides an explanation of how unimolecular reactions can arise.
The overall rate law must be derivable from the mechanism in order for it to be a viable depiction of how the reaction takes place.
In addition to depicting the overall stoichiometry of a reaction, the kinetic mechanism must also give the overall rate law for the reaction.
Variability in rates and extent of completion (or reaching equilibrium) for elementary steps is considered when obtaining the overall rate law from expressions for each elementary step.

Some elementary steps may establish pre-equilibrium with a reactive intermediate, in which case both forward and reverse rate constants for the elementary steps are used in determining the overall rate law.
Reaction intermediates that build up may require an induction period before they reach a stable concentration.
The steady state approximation may be invoked to determine the overall rate law for mechanisms that produce reaction intermediates.
Reaction mechanisms cannot be generally proven, but observation of reactive intermediates is capable of providing important supporting evidence for a proposed mechanism.
For many/most reaction mechanisms, one elementary step is much slower than others and largely determines the overall rate.
The slow step in a reaction mechanism determines the overall rate of the reaction as is called the rate determining step.
Chemical intermediates are often important in reactions and the lifetime of intermediates dictates the observation time-scale.
Relatively long lived intermediates are often formed by a pre-equilibrium process prior to a rate determining step.
Methods exist to observe kinetics on a state-to-state level.
Experimental techniques can be used to cool molecules to limit the number of rotational and vibrational states occupied by reactants.
Experimental probes, such as laser induced fluorescence, may be able to measure rotational and vibrational states of the products of a reaction.
Typically for small molecular systems, initial vibrational states may be selected to be excited to determine state-to-state effects on reaction dynamics.
Atmospheric chemistry, including pollution formation, is usually described with a complicated kinetic mechanism.

Reactions in the upper atmosphere tend to have low collision frequencies because of the low pressures, and mechanisms proposed in such regions must account for how energy is removed from the reacting system by subsequent collisions.
A number of atmospheric processes are initiated by sunlight, so photochemical elementary steps are often an important component of the reaction mechanisms in the atmosphere.
Models that accurately account for the formation of key pollutants, like lung irritants, may include hundreds of elementary reactions.
In biochemical systems, many reactions take place in cycles, and the kinetics of the overall process depends on the rate of the steps.

Obtaining energy as part of cellular respiration involves the Krebs cycle, and the kinetics of each step in the cycle must be studied to understand the rate of the overall process and the effects of enzymes and other factors on that rate.

The study of the rate at which pharmaceutical molecules are metabolized and removed from the body is vital to the medical effectiveness of the treatment, and forms the basis of the field of pharmacokinetics.

D.text: An elementary reaction requires that the reactants collide (interact) and have both enough energy and appropriate orientation of colliding particles for the reaction to occur.

lens_texts.general: An elementary reaction requires that the reactants collide (interact) and have both enough energy and appropriate orientation of colliding particles for the reaction to occur.
lens_texts.organic: An elementary reaction requires that the reactants collide (interact) and have both enough energy and appropriate orientation of colliding particles for the reaction to occur.
lens_texts.inorganic: An elementary reaction requires that the reactants collide (interact) and have both enough energy and appropriate orientation of colliding particles for the reaction to occur
lens_texts.physical: An elementary reaction requires that the reactants collide (interact) and have both enough energy and appropriate orientation of colliding particles for the reaction to occur.

1.text: The collision theory of reactions indicates that collisions result in products only if there is enough energy and if the orientation of the reactants is appropriate.

a.text: The number of particles involved in a collision defines the reaction as unimolecular, bimolecular, or termolecular.

b.text: At the molecular scale, reactions are required to overcome an energy barrier, called the activation energy, in order to take place.

2.text: The energy required to initiate a reaction is called the activation energy.

a.text: In many cases, overcoming the activation energy is achieved by high - speed collisions between rapidly moving molecules in a sample.

organic.text: Transition state theory is used mainly to explain kinetics in SN2 reactions.

inorganic.text: Collisions occurring in aqueous solutions often involve a pre-arrangement within spheres or cages of water molecules.

physical.text: Molecular collisions lead to products through an activated complex. The relative energy of this complex dictates the activation energy.
All reactions involve a collision between reacting molecules.
When reacting molecules are in the act of colliding, they form a transient species called an activated complex, from which the reaction may or may not proceed to products.
The molecular scale definition of the activation energy is the amount of energy that the activated complex is higher than the reactants.
Kinetic molecular theory uses the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution to describe the distribution of speeds of particles in a sample.
Gas kinetic theory begins with a set of postulates that describe the behavior of gases at the molecular scale.
The Maxell-Boltzmann distribution is temperature dependent and describes the fraction of particles moving at a particular velocity.
Integration of the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution over all velocities must be equal to one because the probability must be 100% that any given particle has some velocity between zero and infinity.
Integration over the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution from some velocity to infinity provides the fraction of molecules that exceed that velocity.

The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of the gas and for the Boltzmann-Maxwell distribution relationships can enumerate the average speed, the root mean square speed and the most probable speed.
Because kinetic energy depends on mass, heavier molecules will move slower than lighter molecules at the same temperature.
The mass dependence of the velocity distribution affects diffusion and effusion rates and as a result presents a way to measure the molar mass of a gas.
Temperature, pressure, volume, concentration and composition can influence collision rates and the mean free path.
The mean free path is the average distance that a gas molecule travels between collisions and it is inversely proportional to the collision frequency.
The collision energy is dictated by the relative velocities of the colliding particles.
Higher temperatures increase reaction rates because more molecules have higher velocities that lead to more energetic collisions.
Increased pressure at constant temperature leads to increased concentration which increases the number of molecular collisions.
The mean free path is inversely related to the number of particles per unit volume, so changing the volume without changing the number of particles will alter the mean free path.
Collision theory and transition state theory provide numerical models relating molecular scale dynamics to macroscopic reaction rates.
Collision theory describes the rate of reaction in terms of collision frequency, a steric factor, the activation energy and the temperature.
Even reactions that have enough energy to overcome the activation energy may not lead to a reaction.
The steric factor in collision theory accounts for the fact that the relative orientation of colliding molecules may affect whether or not a given collision will lead to reaction.
Transition state theory assumes that reactants reach a quasi-equilibrium with the activated complex in order to derive the expression for the rate of reaction.
The rate constant in transition state theory is proportional to an exponential of the free energy of activation.

E.text: Catalysis increases the rate of reaction and has important applications in a number of subdisciplines of chemistry.

lens_texts.general: Catalysis increases the rate of reaction and has important applications in a number of subdisciplines of chemistry.
lens_texts.organic: Catalysis increases the rate of reaction and has important applications in a number of subdisciplines of chemistry.
lens_texts.inorganic: Catalysis increases the rate of reaction and has important applications in a number of sub-disciplines of chemistry
lens_texts.physical: Catalysis increases the rate of reaction and has important applications in a number of sub-disciplines of chemistry.

1.text: A catalyst is defined as an agent that increases the rate of the reaction while not being consumed by the reaction.

a.text: Catalysts can be either homogeneous or heterogeneous.

b.text: Catalysts play an important role in applications, such as catalytic converters on cars, or environmental events, such as ozone depletion.

2.text: A catalyst increases the rate of the reaction by providing a new reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.

a.text: Catalysts provide an alternative reaction pathway that lowers this activation energy.

b.text: Because a catalyst lowers the activation energy, it affects both forward and reverse reactions.

organic.text: Catalysis changes the path of a reaction to a lower activation energy, which can be shown through changes in the reaction rates.

inorganic.text: Catalysts influence reaction orientation and pathway, leading to an alteration of the potential energy surface and decrease in activation energy for the reaction.
A catalytic cycle is a mechanism proposed to explain the formation of products and regeneration of the active catalyst.
Catalysts for reactions are chosen based on their activity, selectivity, and lifetime.
Turnover frequencies and turnover numbers can be used to compare the activity of different catalysts.
The structure of a heterogeneous catalyst can influence the activity and selectivity of a reaction.

Activity of a catalyst increases with increased surface area. This can be accomplished physically by supporting the catalyst on a high surface area substrate, or synthetically using reaction conditions, as is done with zeolites.
Many reactions involving heterogeneous catalysts involve interaction with acidic and/or basic sites on the catalyst surface.
The porous structure of zeolites can be used to impart shape selectivity in various reactions.
Reactions of homogeneous catalysts are often studied as models for processes occurring in heterogeneous systems.

physical.text: A catalyst changes the reaction mechanism and the new mechanism has a lower overall activation energy than the uncatalyzed pathway.
Because the new pathway provided by a catalyst lowers the activation energy, it speeds the overall reaction.
Catalysis may occur in a single phase (homogeneous) or at a phase interface (heterogeneous).
Homogeneous catalysis may allow for desirable features such as asymmetric synthesis, but typically has greater challenges separating the products and the catalyst once a reaction has occurred.
Heterogeneous catalysis by solids occurs when reactive species chemisorb on the surface and the adsorbed species react then desorb.
Two key mechanisms for solid surface catalysis are the Langmuir-Hinshelwood and the Eley- Rideal mechanisms.
Electrochemical catalysis is a special category of heterogeneous catalysis that takes place at the surface of an electrode.
Enzyme catalysis is a critical component of many biochemical reactions.
The Michaelis-Menten mechanism provides a key model for understanding substrate binding in enzyme catalysis.
Specific mechanisms for enzyme activity are strongly dependent on the structure of the enzyme and the ligand.

F.text: Reaction products can be influenced by controlling whether reaction rate or reaction energy plays the key role in the mechanism.

lens_texts.general: Reaction products can be influenced by controlling whether reaction rate or reaction energy plays the key role in the mechanism.
lens_texts.organic: Reaction products can be influenced by controlling whether reaction rate or reaction energy plays the key role in the mechanism.
lens_texts.inorganic: Reaction products can be influenced by controlling whether reaction rate or reaction energy plays the key role in the mechanism
lens_texts.physical: Reaction products can be influenced by controlling whether reaction rate or reaction energy plays the key role in the mechanism.

1.text: When reaction rate is the dominating factor for an observed process , it is said to be kinetically favored. When reaction energy is the dominating factor , it is said to be thermodynamically favored.

a.text: Observing changes over time can sometimes distinguish between kinetically and thermodynamically favored processes.

organic.text: Kinetic versus thermodynamic control of a reaction and reaction coordinate diagrams are used to discuss how to control the reaction products.
The role of reaction intermediates and concepts such as resonance and hyperconjugation inform the manner in which this type of reaction control is understood.

inorganic.text: The identification of kinetic vs. thermodynamic product as a function of the reaction is important to the understanding of a reaction mechanism.
Kinetic products are often isolated and later converted into thermodynamic products.
Kinetic factors, such as overpotential, can be used to control the observed products obtained from oxidation-reduction reactions.

physical.text: When thermodynamic control is present only the amount of products not the products themselves can be adjusted.
Catalysts, in particular, do not influence the equilibrium thermodynamic position of a reaction.

VIII.title: Equilibrium
VIII.text: Equilibrium: All physical and chemical changes are, in principle, reversible and often reach a state of dynamic equilibrium.

A.text: Both physical and chemical changes may occur in either direction (e.g., from reactants to products, or products to reactants).

lens_texts.general: Both physical and chemical changes may occur in either direction (e.g., from reactants to products, or products to reactants).

1.text: Phase changes are reversible and provide a good example of dynamic equilibrium.

a.text: Interpretation of phase diagrams can be tied to the understanding of equilibrium concepts.

organic.text: The position of equilibrium can affect the amount of product formed by a reaction.
Enols and enolate ions are in equilibrium with their respective ketones or aldehydes.

inorganic.text: Microscopic reversibility is important in the understanding of reaction coordinate diagrams for a variety of reaction mechanisms.

physical.text: Depending on conditions, either physical or chemical changes may be observed to proceed in either a "forward" or "reverse" direction, as defined by the chemical equation for the process.

Because reactions or physical changes may proceed in either direction, the equation describing a process is in some sense arbitrary, but the designation of the forward direction has implications on the details of the quantitative description of the system.

B.text: When opposing processes both occur at the same rate, the net change is zero.

lens_texts.general: When opposing processes both occur at the same rate, the net change is zero.
lens_texts.organic: When opposing processes both occur at the same rate the net change is zero.

1.text: Dynamic processes that achieve equilibrium may be phase changes or chemical reactions.

a.text: Concentration versus time profiles can be used to demonstrate kinetic versus equilibrium realm.

b.text: Equilibrium is dynamic because rates of opposing process are the same, but the rate is not commonly zero.

organic.text: Reversible reactions reach equilibrium.

inorganic.text: Equilibrium represents a steady state created by a dynamic process of forward and reverse processes.
A system is at equilibrium when the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal.

physical.text: Equilibrium is dynamic despite the observation that there is no net change.
Even when no net change in composition is observed for a system, processes in opposing directions are occurring, but at the same rate, leading to dynamic equilibrium.
For some reactions, the energy required to induce the reverse reaction is so large that it is impractical to attempt to observe equilibrium concentrations of reactants.
While, in principle, all reactions reach equilibrium, some reactions proceed so strongly towards products as to make observation of the reverse reaction impractical.

C.text: For chemical and physical processes, the equilibrium state can be characterized via the equilibrium constant.

lens_texts.general: For chemical and physical processes, the equilibrium state can be characterized via the equilibrium constant.
lens_texts.organic: For chemical reactions, the equilibrium state can be characterized via the equilibrium constant.
lens_texts.inorganic: For chemical reactions, the equilibrium state can be characterized via the equilibrium constant.
lens_texts.physical: For chemical reactions, the equilibrium state can be characterized via the equilibrium constant.

1.text: The equilibrium constant can be used in calculations that determine the amount of reactants or products present at equilibrium for a given initial state.

a.text: The equilibrium state is characterized by a constant, designated K, which provides quantitative information of the extent of a reaction and is related to the ratio of the concentrations of reactants and products.

b.text: The equilibrium constant, K, is a function of temperature.

c.text: The equilibrium constant, K, incorporates reaction stoichiometry as part of the ratio.

d.text: Calculations using equilibrium constants may determine K, or estimate equilibrium concentrations given initial concentrations of a system with a known value of K.

2.text: Solubility of solids, particularly ionic solids, provides an example of chemical equilibrium.

a.text: Dissolving of solids in water provides an example of equilibrium systems, for which quantitative understanding via Ksp can be derived.

b.text: There are limitations related to using molarity as the unit of concentration in this type of equilibrium problem, so answers obtained are subject to error.

organic.text: An equilibrium state can be shown using a reaction-coordinate diagram, by performing a conformational analysis or using instrumentation.
pKa is a measure of the equilibrium between the protonated and deprotonated forms of a molecule.

Terminal alkyne hydrogens are more acidic (pKa ≈25) than most C–H bonds due to the s-character of the hybrid orbital (sp) containing the conjugate base lone pair. Deprotonated terminal alkynes are good nucleophiles.
The acidity of phenols is the result of resonance stabilization within the aromatic ring of the conjugate base’s negative charge.

Alpha-hydrogens to carbonyl groups are acidic due to resonance stabilization of the conjugate base (i.e., an enolate). Enolates can be used as nucleophiles and therefore can be involved in any nucleophilic reaction (e.g., aldol or Claisen condensation).
Any H on an O is more acidic than carbon or nitrogen due to the ability of O to handle a negative charge.

inorganic.text: Standard equilibrium constants are used to describe many reaction types.

The acid dissociation constant (Ka) and base ionization constant (Kb) are used to compare the strengths of acids and bases. The Hammett acidity function can also be used to compare strengths of superacids.
Autoionization constants are used to describe ionization equilibria resulting from reaction between solvent molecules.
The dissolution of ionic solids results in an equilibrium described by the solubility product (Ksp).

Complexation equilibria are described using formation constants (Kf) and dissociation constants (Kd). Different expressions of these constants are used to represent stepwise and overall formation/dissociation of the corresponding metal complexes.

physical.text: Equilibrium occurs when free energy is minimized.
The reaction Gibbs energy is defined as the partial derivative of the Gibbs energy with respect to extent of reaction at constant pressure and temperature.
Equilibrium is reached in a chemical reaction when the reaction Gibbs energy becomes zero.

The direction a reaction will proceed can be inferred from the initial reaction Gibbs energy, where a negative value means the forward reaction is the spontaneous direction and a positive value means the reverse reaction is the spontaneous direction.
Equilibrium states occur when the chemical potentials of the involved components are equal.
Because the reaction Gibbs energy is the chemical potential of the products minus that of the reactants, it goes to zero and equilibrium is reached when those chemical potentials are equal.
The reaction will proceed towards products whenever the chemical potential of the reactants is greater than that of the products and vice-versa.
Equilibrium constants are defined in terms of the activity/fugacity of the species in the reactions.

The reaction quotient is defined as the activities (fugacity for gases) of products raised to their stoichiometric coefficient divided by the activities/fugacities of the reactants raised to their stoichiometric coefficients.
When equilibrium is reached, the reaction quotient is equal to the equilibrium constant.
The stoichiometric coefficients arise in the equilibrium constant because the extent of reaction inherently incorporates them.

D.text: When the equilibrium constant is very large or small, products or reactants, respectively, are primarily present at equilibrium. Systems with K near 1 have significant amounts of both reactants and products present.

lens_texts.general: When the equilibrium constant is very large or small, products or reactants, respectively, are primarily present at equilibrium. Systems with K near 1 have significant amounts of both reactants and products present.
lens_texts.organic: When the equilibrium constant is very large or small, products or reactants, respectively, are primarily present at equilibrium. Systems with K near 1 have significant amounts of both reactants and products present.
lens_texts.inorganic: When the equilibrium constant is very large or small, products or reactants (respectively) are primarily present at equilibrium. Systems with K near 1 have significant amounts of both reactants and products present.

1.text: Very large or very small values of the equilibrium constant, K, indicate reactions strongly favoring products (in the former case) or reactants (in the latter).

a.text: Reactions with very small values of K will have little formation of products, while reactions with very large values of K will proceed nearly completely to products.

2.text: Because the equilibrium constant is determined for the reaction as written, the reverse reaction has the inverse equilibrium constant.

a.text: Strong acids have very large K values and are considered fully ionized; weak acids have small K values and are only partially ionized.

b.text: For some reactions, particular acid–base chemistry, the concept of pKa, pKb , or pKw can both illustrate the relationship between the equilibrium constant of forward and reverse reactions, and provide qualitative reasoning for reaction extents.

c.text: Ksp values can be used to rank relative solubilities for sparingly soluble salts, or obtain numerical estimates of measureable solubility of these salts.

3.text: The equilibrium constant for a series of reactions is the product of the individual equilibrium constants.

a.text: Qualitative analysis methods, such as the formation of complex ions, take advantage of differences in Ksp or combined equilibrium constants to separate species dissolved in water.

organic.text: When the equilibrium constant K is very large, product formation is strongly favored.

inorganic.text: Relative sizes of equilibrium constants are used to describe periodic trends in properties.
Hard-Soft Acid-Base Theory can be used to rationalize the magnitudes of many equilibrium constants.

physical.text: The magnitude of the equilibrium constant indicates the propensity of the formation of reactants versus products for a reaction.
Because K = SUM [products]^n /SUM [reactants]^m, the value becomes very large if mostly products are present and very small if mostly reactants are present.
Systems with intermediate values of K will have significant amounts of both reactants and products present at equilibrium.
For similar systems, such as acid/base chemistry or precipitations, the propensity of chemical systems can be ranked based on the size of equilibrium constants.
Some reactions are product favored while others are reactant favored based on the value of their standard state free energy of formation and chemical potentials of the chemicals involved.
The standard state free energy reflects the difference between the chemical potentials of reactants and products, and thus indicates the expected direction of a chemical reaction.

E.text: If perturbed, a system at equilibrium will respond in the direction that tends to offset the perturbation.

lens_texts.general: If perturbed, a system at equilibrium will respond in the direction that tends to offset the perturbation.
lens_texts.organic: If perturbed, a system at equilibrium will respond in the direction that tends to offset the perturbation.
lens_texts.inorganic: If perturbed, a system at equilibrium will respond in the direction that tends to offset the perturbation.
lens_texts.physical: If perturbed, a system at equilibrium will respond in the direction that tends to offset the perturbation.

1.text: The direction of change in a system that is perturbed from equilibrium is predictable—it will change so as to minimize the perturbation.

a.text: The ability to predict the direction a reaction will progress for a given perturbation is a key concept.

b.text: Reasoning based on perturbations of equilibrium can be used to determine conditions that maximize product formation in a reaction.

organic.text: It is possible to use Le Châtelier’s principle to force a reaction to form product.

inorganic.text: Industrial processes often use excess reactants, high pressures, and high temperatures to exploit LeChatelier's principle to favor product formation in reactions that have a high activation energy and/or result in a decrease in the number of gas molecules.
The Haber-Bosch process is used to synthesize ammonia from hydrogen and nitrogen at high temperatures and pressures using an iron based catalyst.
The contact process is used in the production of sulfuric acid to oxidize sulfur dioxide into sulfur trioxide at high temperatures and pressures using a vanadium(V) catalyst.

physical.text: The perturbation of the equilibrium system changes the chemical potential of at least one component, so chemical potential is no longer equal and equilibrium is not present.
When the chemical potentials are rendered not equal by a change in conditions, the reaction will proceed in a direction that allows them to regain the equality.
Temperature-based perturbations to equilibrium change the value of K.
A system will reestablish equilibrium with a new value for K when the temperature is changed.

F.text: Thermodynamics provides mathematical tools to understand equilibrium systems quantitatively.

lens_texts.general: Thermodynamics provides mathematical tools to understand equilibrium systems quantitatively.
lens_texts.organic: Thermodynamics provides mathematical tools to understand equilibrium systems quantitatively.
lens_texts.inorganic: Thermodynamics provides mathematical tools to understand equilibrium systems quantitatively.
lens_texts.physical: Thermodynamics provides mathematical tools to understand equilibrium systems quantitatively.

1.text: The equilibrium constant is related mathematically to the change in free energy.

a.text: Calculations of the equilibrium constant of a system from the free energy of that system are important.

b.text: Systems achieve equilibrium when free energy is minimized.

2.text: For electrochemical systems, the cell potential is also related to the change in free energy.

inorganic.text: Equilibrium constants and their connection to ΔG, ΔH, ΔS and E° are important in understanding quantitative measures of stability and reactivity.

The values for the electrical cell potential and the Gibbs free energy can be used to determine if a system is at equilibrium, and the direction of change that a system needs to undergo to attain equilibrium.
The proton gain enthalpy and proton affinity are often used to aid in the understanding of Bronsted acid strength.
Thermodynamic concepts are important in the understanding of the formation and reactivity of coordination compounds.
The strengths of metal-ligand bonds, acidity/basicity of ligands, and solvent interactions are important factors in equilibria involving complex ions.
The relative frontier molecular orbital energies of reactants can be used to predict the extent of electron transfer in Lewis acid-base and oxidation-reduction reactions.
The chelate and macrocycle effects cause equilibrium constants for the formation of complexes containing chelating ligands to be large.

physical.text: The condition that the sum of chemical potentials must equal each other at equilibrium allows the derivation of several important relationships.
Keq relates to ΔH and ΔS and thus ΔG.
The relationships between the equilibrium constant and free energy arise from statistical mechanics but can derived without it.
The overall equilibrium constant is defined in terms of the ΔG of the reaction.
The standard free energy is related to the equilibrium constant by the equation, ∆G° = -RT ln(K)
The van't Hoff equation describes how equilibrium constants depend on temperature.

G.text: Equilibrium concepts have important applications in several subdisciplines of chemistry.

lens_texts.general: Equilibrium concepts have important applications in several subdisciplines of chemistry.
lens_texts.organic: Equilibrium concepts have important applications in several subdisciplines of chemistry.

1.text: Many reactions categorized as acid–base are described via equilibrium.

a.text: Acid–base chemistry, particularly in water, forms an important example of equilibrium systems. Conceptual and quantitative understanding of this form of equilibrium system is important.

b.text: The laboratory technique of titration serves as a key example for acid– base chemistry; interpretation of titration curves, both conceptually and quantitatively, is an important tool for chemists.

c.text: pH is used in quantitative descriptions of acid–base chemistry.

d.text: Conjugate bases of weak acids are strong, and conjugate acids of weak bases are strong. Thus, salts of weak acids and bases affect pH.

2.text: Buffers resist changes in pH because both the acid and base of a conjugate pair are present.

a.text: Weak acid–base systems are capable of forming buffer systems that tend to resist changes in the pH of the system.

b.text: Conceptual and quantitative understanding of buffers is important.

3.text: Protein–substrate binding can serve as another example of the application of equilibrium concepts.

organic.text: Protonation of functional groups in organic molecules is an equilibrium process (and it is essential to acid-catalyzed processes, for example).
Brønsted acids are proton donors; bases are proton acceptors. Lewis acids are electron-pair acceptors; Lewis bases are electron-pair donors.
The reversibility of many reactions is important in understanding mechanisms and in predicting reaction outcomes.

inorganic.text: Equilibrium constants can be used to determine the reactivity of inorganic compounds.
The levelling effect can be used to control acid-base behavior in different solvent systems.

Chemical speciation is dependent on a number of factors. The position of a chemical equilibrium depends on many conditions, including pH, temperature, pressure, and the presence of oxidizing/reducing agents.
Distribution diagrams are used to describe the speciation of acid-base species as a function of solution pH.
Phase diagrams can be used to determine the most stable form of a compound as a function of temperature and pressure.
Chemical sensors use chemical equilibria to quantify the amount of analyte present.

physical.text: Equilibrium plays an important role in many biochemical systems.
The binding and unbinding of oxygen to hemoglobin is an equilibrium process that illustrates the role of equilibrium in biochemistry.
In some cases, adsorption and reactions at surfaces may be described by equilibrium principles.
Gases are in equilibrium with adsorbed species that may or may not dissociate.

IX.title: Experiments, Measurement, and Data
IX.text: Experiments, Measurement, and Data: Chemistry is generally advanced via experimental observations.

A.text: Materials are frequently mixtures of chemical substances.

lens_texts.general: Materials are frequently mixtures of chemical substances.
lens_texts.organic: Quantitative observation of matter can be made at a wide range of distance and/or time scales.
lens_texts.inorganic: Quantitative observation of matter can be made at a wide range of distance scales and/or time scales.
lens_texts.physical: Quantitative observation of matter can be made at a wide range of distance scales, energy, frequency and/or time scales.

1.text: Mixtures may be homogeneous or heterogeneous.

a.text: Macroscopic samples of everyday objects and systems can serve as examples of homogeneous versus heterogeneous mixtures.

2.text: Methods such as distillation and chromatography can be used to separate mixtures.

a.text: A simple distillation apparatus can be used to separate mixtures in the laboratory.

organic.text: Data collected can be measured at the macroscopic level using chemical tests.
Data collected can be measured at the microscopic level using instruments such as X-ray, NMR, IR, MS, and EPR.
Wet chemical methods may take time to provide results and results may be unclear due to multiple functional groups, particularly when compared with instrumental methods.

inorganic.text: Microscopy allows for the observation of matter from the macroscopic to the atomic levels.
Optical microscopy allows for observation of matter at resolutions above 0.2 microns.
Nanoscale structures can be viewed using transmission and scanning electron microscopies.
Scanning probe microscopy can be used to observe structures on the atomic/molecular size scales. Examples of probe microscopy include scanning tunneling microscopy and atomic force microscopy.
Fluxional processes in molecules can be observed at many timescales using spectroscopic techniques.
Many molecular rearrangements take place on the same timescale as the NMR experiment, and dynamic NMR experiments can be used to obtain thermodynamic and kinetic information for these processes.
Techniques employing pulsed lasers can be used to observe bond stretching and molecular vibrations occurring on the femtosecond timescale.
Structural information for a molecule, including bond lengths and bond angles, is based on observations of samples made at the macroscopic level.
The connectivity and structure of a molecule can be obtained using one- and two-dimensional NMR techniques.
Infrared spectroscopy can be used to determine functional groups present and bond strengths within a molecule, and is commonly used in the identification of compounds containing carbonyl ligands.
X-ray crystallography can be used to determine bond lengths and angles within a compound.
Phosphorescence and Fluorescence phenomena occur at different timescales due to the different relaxation mechanisms taking place within a molecule.

physical.text: Diffraction requires the wavelength of light/particles to be on the order of the spacing between particles to be observed.
X-rays represent a good tool for observations at the atomic scale because the wavelength is roughly equivalent to interatomic distances in solids.
The method of observation in kinetics has to be sensitive to time-scale of observation.
Femtosecond spectroscopy provides the fastest time scale for the study of reaction kinetics.
Temperature jump methods can access kinetics in the microsecond time range.
Shock tube methods provide conditions that allow the study of reactions on the millisecond time scale.
Most kinetics are observed based on collections of a large number of reactions, but individual collisions can be observed in crossed-molecular beams.

B.text: Quantitative observation of matter can be made at a wide range of distance, energy, frequency, and/or time scales.

lens_texts.general: Quantitative observation of matter can be made at a wide range of distance, energy, frequency, and/or time scales.
lens_texts.organic: Because there are a large number of compounds, a system of naming these compounds is used.
lens_texts.inorganic: Because there are a large number of compounds, a system of naming these compounds is used.
lens_texts.physical: Because there are a large number of compounds, a system of naming these compounds is used.

1.text: Laboratory observations are made and then often understood in terms of particulate-level models.

a.text: While molecular-scale observations are not generally made in the introductory chemistry laboratory, interpretation of results often invokes molecular-scale reasoning.

b.text: Historically, the development of the atomic theory of matter was driven by experimental observations.

2.text: Laboratory measurements are sometimes combined into ratios; for example, density is measured via a ratio of mass and volume.

a.text: Calculations that use density may include both the determination of the density from mass/volume data or the use of a known density with the measurement of either mass or volume.

b.text: Practical implications for density include the concept of buoyancy.

3.text: Laboratory observation of reaction rates helps to establish the concept of reaction time scales empirically.

a.text: Rate laws and reaction order are determined using empirical rate data.

organic.text: In order to be able to organize observations on vast numbers of compounds, a systematic nomenclature system has been devised to name compounds.
IUPAC has outlined a set of systematic guidelines for naming all organic structures based on carbon chain length, rings, functional groups, and substituents.
Hydrocarbons contain carbon and hydrogen atoms. Hydrocarbons with only carbon–carbon single bonds are called alkanes; they can be straight-chained or branched.
Substituents on a di-substituted benzene ring can be labeled as ortho, meta, or para to each other.

inorganic.text: The nomenclature system for coordination and organometallic compounds is used to specifies composition and stereochemistry.
The systematic name of a coordination compound includes information about the number and type of ligands along with the oxidation state of the metal ion.
One type of stereoisomerism, geometric isomerism, has special nomenclature associated with it. Examples include cis/trans isomers and mer/fac isomers.

Many ligands have multiple binding modes that should also be specified within the name of the corresponding complex. Examples include the κ (kappa), η (eta), and μ (mu) designations for denticity, hapticity and bridging ligands and the nomenclature of ambidentate ligands.

Simple crystal structures are often identified by specific names associated with prototypical compounds. The hole concept is used to describe the relative locations of cations and ions within the structures of crystalline ionic compounds.
The cesium chloride structure contains cesium atoms in the cubic holes of a primitive cubic chloride lattice.
The sodium chloride, fluorite, and zinc blende structures contain counterions within the octahedral or tetrahedral holes of a parent cubic-closest-packed lattice.
The nickel arsenide and wurtzite structures contain counterions within the octahedral and tetrahedral holes of a parent hexagonal-closest-packed lattice.
The tetragonal rutile structure can be visualized as having titanium atoms occupying half of the octahedral holes within a distorted hexagonally-closest-packed oxide lattice.
The perovskite and spinel structures are observed in many tertiary ionic compounds.
Many catalysts and industrial processes are identified using common names associated with the people that discovered and/or worked on the development of the process/catalyst.
Students should be able to associate the common name of these compounds with their composition and structure, and the general type of reaction associated.

Homogeneous catalysts are employed in the hydrogenation, hydroformylation, oxidation and metathesis reactions of alkenes. Other common processes include acetic acid synthesis and carbon-carbon bond formation.
Common processes using heterogeneous catalysts include hydrogenation, ammonia synthesis, sulfuric acid synthesis, and alkane synthesis.

C.text: Because there are a large number of compounds, a system of naming these compounds is used.

lens_texts.general: Because there are a large number of compounds, a system of naming these compounds is used.
lens_texts.organic: Experimental control of reactions plays a key role in the synthesis of new materials and analysis of composition.
lens_texts.inorganic: Experimental control of reactions plays a key role in the synthesis of new materials and analysis of composition.

1.text: A system of nomenclature is applied based on the classification of the substance.

a.text: Anyone who works with chemicals needs to be able to name compounds, including binary inorganic compounds, acids, and some organic chemicals.

organic.text: Experimental measures provide data to determine whether desired products are obtained.
Measures of products can include stereochemical specificity.

inorganic.text: The parameters used in a synthesis (relative amounts, temperature, reaction time, pH, light/air/water exposure, etc.) can influence the identity and relative amounts of the product(s) obtained.
Exothermic and endothermic reactions are affected differently by temperature.
Many reactions fall into general reaction classes that have characteristic behavior under changing conditions, and knowledge of these reaction types can be used in the informed design of a synthesis.
Analysis using one or more techniques is used to determine identity and purity of products and understand effect of changing reaction conditions.

physical.text: Laser based photochemical reactions can be controlled in a state to state manner.
Reaction products in laser photochemistry may be influenced by state specific excitation of the reactants.
Insights into controlled synthesis of modern materials, including nanoparticles, often requires detailed understanding of reaction conditions.
Synthesis of nanoparticles requires different reaction controls than traditional bulk chemical reactions.
Understanding the role of solvent polarity in control of a reaction requires knowledge of polarity of product, reactant and intermediate substances.

D.text: Experimental control of reactions plays a key role in the synthesis of new materials and analysis of composition.

lens_texts.general: Experimental control of reactions plays a key role in the synthesis of new materials and analysis of composition.
lens_texts.organic: Chemical measurements are based on mass, charge, or interaction with electrons or photons.
lens_texts.inorganic: Chemical measurements are based on mass, charge, or interaction with electrons or photons.
lens_texts.physical: Chemical measurements are based on mass, charge, temperature, pressure, volume or interaction with electrons or photons.

1.text: One key way to control reactions is to control the amount of reactants by varying concentrations.

a.text: Le Châtelier’s principle is demonstrated by varying the concentration of one species and observing the outcome on the overall reaction.

inorganic.text: The chemical formula of a compound is determined using a combination of analysis techniques.
The elemental composition of compounds is measured using a variety of methods including combustion analysis, atomic absorption, and atomic emission.

The behavior of ions in the presence of an electric field or magnetic field can be a function of the mass of the ion. Mass spectrometric techniques involve analysis of this behavior to identify chemical formulas and presence of common structural fragments within molecules.
The percent yield for an experiment can be calculated from reactant and product masses.
UV-VIS absorption spectroscopy is used to observe valence shell electron transitions within molecules.
Intensity of UV-Vis transition corresponds to type of electronic transition and the concentration of analyte present.
The symmetry of a molecule determines the types of allowed transitions that can occur and hence the intensity of the observed absorption.
A Tanabe-Sugano diagram is used to interpret the energy information obtained from UV-Vis spectroscopy of transition metal compounds.
Multinuclear NMR experiments are used to identify the structures of inorganic complexes.
The number and locations of chemical shifts observed in an NMR spectrum can be used to identify the chemical environments present in a molecule.
Splitting patterns in observed chemical shifts result from interactions with other NMR active nuclei in the molecule.
Redox reactions can be used quantitatively in analysis.
Potentiometric titrations can be used to analyze the composition of reaction mixtures.
The elemental forms of many active metals and nonmetals are obtained using electrolytic methods.
Cyclic voltammetry is commonly used to study redox processes occurring in solution.
Different spectroscopic techniques employ different types of electromagnetic radiation to measure transitions occurring at different energies within molecules.

The energies of microwave radiation correspond to the rotational states of a molecule. More commonly, long wavelength radiation is used in the NMR and EPR experiments to measure transitions occurring between different magnetic spin states of atoms within molecules.

Infrared radiation is used to measure vibrational transitions within molecules. Vibrational transitions are also observed as small deviations from the absorbance of visible light using Raman spectroscopy.
Absorption and emission of light within UV-Visible wavelengths is associated with valence electronic transitions within molecules.

Absorbance and emission of X-rays is usually associated with electronic transitions involving core energy levels, and is used to obtain information about the local environments of atoms within molecules.
Mossbauer spectroscopy involves the absorption of gamma rays to probe the energies associated with nuclear spin levels.

Diffraction methods employing X-rays, electrons, and neutrons are used to measure the interatomic distances within compounds, and information gained from these experiments can be used to obtain bond distances and angles.
Powder diffraction techniques are used to obtain basic structural information about solids including the phases present, crystallinity, and unit cell lattice parameters.
Single crystal diffraction techniques are used to obtain more specific information about unit cell contents and interatomic distances.
Magnetic measurements, including magnetic susceptibility and SQUID measurements, are employed to determine the individual and cooperative behavior of unpaired electrons within a compound.
Temperature dependent conductivity and resistivity measurements are used to characterize metals, semiconductors, and superconductors.
Metals become less conductive at higher temperatures as vibration of electrons interferes with conductance.
Semiconductors become more conductive at higher temperatures as more energy is available to promote electrons to the conductance band.
Superconductors can be so only when a (low) critical temperature is reached allowing Cooper pairs of electrons to form.

physical.text: Interaction of molecules with light is a powerful and routinely used method of molecular observation.
Molecular spectroscopy can provide detailed structural information for small molecule systems.
Spectroscopic frequencies and intensities depend on reduced mass and can be used to distinguish isotope effects.
Spectroscopy may be used to measure changes to physical properties due to adsorption onto surfaces.
Different forms of spectroscopy (IR, Microwave, UV-VIS, PES, Mossbauer, NMR, ESR) examine different aspects of molecules and molecular processes.
Electronic transitions are accessed with UV/visible light.
Vibrational transitions are accessed with IR light.
Pure rotational transitions are accessed with microwave light.
Temperature may be controlled by maintaining constant temperature, or measured to determine temperature effects.
Establishing temperature as a control variable in experiments is commonly accomplished using a constant temperature circulating bath.
Modern experiments often use thermistors or thermocouples to measure temperature and temperature changes.
Electrochemical experiments take advantage of charge and reactions where charge changes are observable by experiments.
Oxidation reduction reactions are an important category of chemical reactions and they may be observed both thermodynamically and kinetically via electrochemical methods.
Mass spectrometry represents an area of experimentation where mass is the primary observation variable.
High resolution mass spectrometry can utilize isotopic abundances to provide detailed identification of reactions.

E.text: Chemical measurements are based on mass, charge, temperature, pressure, volume, or interaction with electrons or photons.

1.text: Stoichiometry provides an example of mass measurements being used in the laboratory, particularly for percentage yield.

a.text: Graphical analysis of reaction yields as a function of reagent amounts can reveal when a particular reactant is in excess and identify an unknown reaction stoichiometric ratio.

b.text: Calculation of percentage yield is an important skill and may help determine the relative utility of a laboratory synthesis method.

2.text: Practical implications of laboratory reactions include the ability to generate species of interest (such as oxygen) or release energy (by combustion of fuels).

a.text: Common laboratory reactions to generate known species, such as oxygen, are an important component of descriptive chemistry.

b.text: Many hydrocarbons can be used as fuels; the combustion of a hydrocarbon in air produces carbon dioxide and water.

3.text: Atomic line spectra provide important evidence that led to the quantum model of the atom.

a.text: Spectral data can be used to demonstrate quantized energy levels in atoms in the gas phase.

4.text: Mass spectrometry can provide data that show the existence of isotopes of elements.

a.text: Mass spectrum data can be used to illustrate the existence of isotopes of an element and the importance of isotopic abundances.

inorganic.text: Demonstration of purity and comparison to peer's results and standards is an essential process.
Magnitudes of many measurements can be sensitive to experimental conditions.

physical.text: Methods can be employed to isolate or reduce complicating variables in experiments.
Vibrational and rotational populations can be collapsed by cooling methods, such as supersonic expansion, to allow state-to-state detection.
Reaction intermediates can be quenched to show their existence even if their reactivity is such that direct observation is difficult.

1.text: Laboratory methods can be devised so that conditions limit the possibilities of measurement errors.

a.text: Techniques in setting up and carrying out laboratory experiments are an important component of instruction in introductory college chemistry.

b.text: Gaining familiarity with laboratory instruments and glassware is a key skill for the development of appropriate laboratory design methods.

c.text: Errors in measurement can occur when techniques (such as meniscus reading or incomplete transfer of chemicals between vessels) arise in the laboratory.

2.text: The preparation of solutions and accurate determination of their concentrations are important components of defining experimental conditions.

a.text: Correct uses of volumetric glassware and/or dilution methods are important techniques in the preparation of solutions for chemical experimentation.

b.text: Determination of solution concentration is often carried out via titration with a standard.

inorganic.text: The precision of measured data has limitations that are dependent on measuring equipment or the execution of the experiment.
Appropriate equipment, including glassware and balances, should be selected to obtain the desired precision for an experiment.
Experimental conditions, including sample preparation for analysis, should be clearly described in the associated procedure.
All relevant data, conditions, and procedures should be recorded in the lab notebook for a particular experiment.

physical.text: Rapid reaction rates call for careful control of laser pulse lengths and/or delays between pulses.
Time delays can be built into laser spectroscopy by beam splitting with one beam going a longer distance.
Kinetic experiments can be designed to observe reaction intermediates.
Reaction intermediates may be measured directly by spectroscopic probes or indirectly using quenching methods.
Experimental data and data analysis can be used to refine or create models and inform chemical systems.
Key experiments in the development of quantum mechanics led to the discovery of wave- particle duality

1.text: Data can be characterized by both accuracy and precision.

a.text: While the words “accuracy” and “precision” can be used nearly interchangeably in everyday life, in the laboratory they have specific meanings that must be understood.

2.text: Error in data can be either random or systematic.

a.text: Significant figures are used to reflect the level of error.

b.text: Standard deviation is relatable to the level of error.

3.text: Proper laboratory procedures record all observations and correct recording errors with cross-outs rather than erasures.

a.text: Appropriate methods for keeping a laboratory notebook are important in the instruction of introductory college chemistry.

4.text: Calibration with samples of known quantities is a common method for determining unknowns in a laboratory setting.

a.text: Construction and use of calibrations curves is an important laboratory skill.

b.text: Standardization of laboratory solutions is a form of calibration that is an important laboratory skill.

inorganic.text: Many experiments in inorganic chemistry are conducted using light, air, and moisture sensitive compounds, and the proper precautions should be employed in their use.
Inert atmosphere techniques employing glove boxes or Schlenk glassware are often used to exclude moisture and/or oxygen from experiments.

Methods for extinguishing fires involving metals and pyrophoric liquids often differ from procedures used to extinguish more common types of fires. When working with these materials, appropriate extinguishing media must be readily accessible.
Experiments conducted at high and low pressures present an explosion hazard, and proper equipment should be selected to minimize the risk of harm from explosion.
Vacuum pumps used to create reduced pressure environments pose an additional risk of injury due to mechanical malfunction, and the proper safeguards should be in place during their use.
Compressed gas cylinders should be secured to avoid injury in case of breach.
Experiments involving cryofluids can pose a risk to burning of the skin or explosions due to the condensation and subsequent reaction of liquid oxygen.

Many resources containing toxicological and other potential safety hazards associated with specific compounds are available and should be consulted prior to working with unfamiliar compounds to ensure that proper safety precautions are being followed.
A fume hood or other method of containment should be used when working with volatile compounds.

Certain classes of compounds require specialized techniques to be utilized and that appropriate first aid measures be on hand in case of exposure. Examples include hydrofluoric acid and hydrogen cyanide

Certain chemicals can react to form harmful byproducts if kept in storage for long periods of time, and special procedures should be developed to catalog and dispose of these compounds. For example, ethers will react with oxygen over long storage times to form shock-sensitive peroxides.

In many cases, a safer alternative compound can be employed to achieve the same desired result in a chemical reaction. One common example is the replacement of perchlorate salts with safer alternatives in syntheses.
Green chemical methods are developed to minimize the environmental impact of an experiment.

physical.text: In addition to chemical risk, physical chemistry experiments often include high vacuum or intense light sources which require proper safety precaution.
Many types of lasers produce light that may harm eyes and appropriate eyewear is required when experiments using them are conducted.

H.text: Chemistry experiments have risks associated with them, so chemical safety is a key consideration in the design of any experiment.

lens_texts.general: Chemistry experiments have risks associated with them, so chemical safety is a key consideration in the design of any experiment.

1.text: Knowledge of appropriate safety apparatus is important knowledge for any work being done in the laboratory.

a.text: Students should be able to identify and use safety equipment in the laboratory.

2.text: Knowledge of chemical hazards and safety procedures associated with chemicals is important in the chemistry laboratory.

a.text: Assessing the hazards associated with chemical procedures, such as the dilution of strong acids or heating of chemicals, is an important skill for introductory chemistry courses.

b.text: Appropriate storage and labeling of chemicals is a constant component of good chemical safety practices. This includes understanding safety terminology and the language, signs, and symbols commonly found in Safety Data Sheets and on labels.

c.text: Basic knowledge about handling of exposure to chemicals due to spills or other accidents is an important component of chemical safety.

d.text: Basic knowledge of and appropriate use of personal protective equipment, such as safety goggles, gloves, and lab coats, are important features of chemical safety.

e.text: Basic knowledge of the possible hazards of chemicals, such as flammability, toxicity, and corrosiveness, is an important component of chemical safety.

f.text: Basic knowledge of the routes of exposure for chemicals, such as inhalation, ingestion, and dermal routes, is an important component of chemical safety.

3.text: Appropriate disposal of chemical waste is a key component of chemical safety and hygiene.

a.text: Appropriate disposal of chemical waste is needed in any laboratory and students should know general guidelines related to chemical waste handling.

4.text: Students should develop an “awareness” of chemical safety when conducting experiments that involves continual consideration of hazards and risks due to chemicals, chemical procedures, and physical hazards that may be present.

a.text: The concept of a “culture of safety” is an increasingly important component of chemical education.

5.text: Radioactive chemicals require additional knowledge related to risks and use of radioactive materials must include appropriate protective measures.

a.text: Exposure to different forms of radiation pose different levels of risk, and students should have a general knowledge of these differences.

A.text: Many theoretical models are constructed at the particulate level, while many empirical observations are made at the macroscopic level.
